attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post. The quoted material that follows it is separate.

semantics.note: Keeps 'often', 'start out great' and 'end badly' as a general observation of a pattern. Swapping 'great' for 'well' makes no material difference.

contract.note: A plain reading of 'often' as a recurring pattern with no numerical threshold is fair. The October 1–21 anchor is narrow for a general pattern, but earlier project histories are allowed, so it does not decide the result.

evidence.note: A literature review published July 2026, before the cutoff. It reports short-term prototype gains and little study of long-horizon outcomes. That is an evidence gap, not a measured frequency of good starts ending badly.

reviews.rationale: The packet contains no longitudinal sample or project histories with a denominator. The only item is a review that names the lack of long-horizon outcome data. The evidence neither shows that initially promising projects commonly fail nor that such failures are rare.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. 'That' points back to his own earlier claims about reliability, demos and maintenance.

semantics.note: Captures the referent of 'that' (unreliable, not suited to complex apps). It leaves out the maintainability item, a minor omission. It is an observation about customers' current recognition.

contract.note: Reading 'figuring out' as a pullback tied to these limits is fair, because Marcus cites declining usage straight away as support. The period chosen from context (June–October 2025) is reasonable.

evidence.note: Barclays figures, reported secondhand, put Lovable traffic down 40% by September. This supports only the pullback part. No cause is given.
Replit reported fast ARR growth by September 2025. This is a company-reported, unaudited disclosure, and it cuts against a broad customer pullback.
The Lovable CEO's claim of >100% net dollar retention is a company statement made in November 2025, after the target period. Context only.

reviews.rationale: Traffic fell at some platforms, but no evidence connects that fall to customers recognizing reliability or complexity limits. Replit's company-reported revenue growth points the other way. Customer belief, which is the core of the claim, is not settled by the packet.

attribution.note: Marcus recalls his own earlier prediction and presents it as vindicated, which is an endorsement.

semantics.note: He restates his earlier claim as a present observation. The context implies amateur vibe coding; the target 'vibe coding tools' roughly keeps that scope.

contract.note: Accepting evidence on AI-generated code in general widens the scope beyond amateur vibe coding. The contract says so openly and applies it both ways, so it is acceptable, but the scope choice affects how much weight the counterevidence gets.

evidence.note: Reports OX vendor research: an over-specification anti-pattern producing hard-to-maintain systems in 80–90% of AI code. Vendor research reported secondhand.
Same OX report: refactoring is avoided in 80–90% of AI code, building technical debt.
InfoQ coverage of the same OX report. It is not independent corroboration.
A controlled experiment found no degradation in maintainability. Its participants were mostly professionals using AI help on one feature, which is far from amateur vibe coding.

reviews.rationale: OX's vendor analysis supports maintainability problems in code that is largely AI-generated. The Borg et al. controlled study found no maintainability penalty when professionals co-develop with AI. The claim holds for heavily AI-generated repositories but is not shown for professional AI-assisted work.

attribution.note: Marcus's own causal assertion in his post.

semantics.note: A firm causal claim. The revised wording correctly keeps 'as always' and avoids overstating it as total inability.

contract.note: Reading 'as always' as a recurring mechanism, rather than the only cause of every failure, is fair. Requiring evidence that separates unfamiliarity from difficulty is reasonable for a causal claim.

evidence.note: Qualitative accounts of breakdowns linked to knowledge cutoffs and private code are consistent with the mechanism. They do not measure its causal share.
Models fail even on library versions released before their cutoffs. That cuts against unseen data being the only explanation, but actual training exposure is unverified.

reviews.rationale: No controlled study in the packet separates training-distribution unfamiliarity from other causes of vibe-coding failure. The qualitative and benchmark evidence points both ways and does not settle the general causal claim.
